The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $(\mathsf X,\Sigma_X)$, $(\mathsf Y,\Sigma_Y)$, and $(\mathsf A,\Sigma_A)$ be nonempty measurable spaces. A **source/target pair of joint laws** consists of probability measures $P_S$ and $P_T$ on $(\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y,\Sigma_X\otimes\Sigma_Y)$. For $D\in\{S,T\}$, its input marginal is the probability measure $\mu_D$ on $(\mathsf X,\Sigma_X)$ defined by $\mu_D(A)=P_D(A\times\mathsf Y)$. If $h:\mathsf X\to\mathsf A$ is measurable and $\ell:\mathsf A\times\mathsf Y\to[0,+\infty]$ is product-measurable, then $(x,y)\mapsto(h(x),y)$ is measurable: the preimage of a measurable rectangle $U\times V$ is $h^{-1}(U)\times V$, and such rectangles generate the product sigma-algebra. Taking preimages once more shows that $(x,y)\mapsto\ell(h(x),y)$ is measurable. The domain risk is the extended nonnegative integral
$$R_D(h):=\int_{\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y}\ell(h(x),y)\,P_D(d(x,y)).$$

A **conditional label kernel** for $P_D$ is a specified probability kernel $K_D$ from $(\mathsf X,\Sigma_X)$ to $(\mathsf Y,\Sigma_Y)$ such that, for every nonnegative product-measurable $g:\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y\to[0,+\infty]$,
$$\int g(x,y)\,P_D(d(x,y))=\int_{\mathsf X}\left(\int_{\mathsf Y}g(x,y)\,K_D(x,dy)\right)\mu_D(dx).$$
The pair is under **covariate shift** when conditional label kernels $K_S,K_T$ are supplied, there is a measurable set $N$ with $\mu_T(N)=0$ such that $K_S(x,\cdot)=K_T(x,\cdot)$ as probability measures for every $x\notin N$, and $\mu_T\ll\mu_S$. No existence of conditional kernels is asserted by this definition.

Let $\mathcal E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be dominated by the fixed sigma-finite positive measure $\mu$. For each
$\theta$, the Radon–Nikodym theorem gives the almost-everywhere class
$dP_\theta/d\mu$; a sigma-finite exhaustion for $\mu$ is also finite for the
probability measure $P_\theta$. Under AC, select simultaneously a
finite-valued measurable nonnegative representative $p_\theta$ from each
class. The nonnegative version exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].

For fixed observed $x\in\mathcal X$, the function
$$L_x:\Theta\to[0,+\infty),\qquad L_x(\theta):=p_\theta(x),$$
is the **likelihood at $x$**. This is a function on the parameter labels, not
a probability distribution on $\Theta$. No sigma-algebra on $\Theta$ or
measurability of $L_x$ is implied. Each density is determined only
$\mu$-almost everywhere; there is no canonical pointwise version and, for
arbitrary uncountable $\Theta$, no common exceptional null set is asserted.

Let $P_0$ and $P_1$ be probability measures on the same measurable space.
Assume AC. Their Lebesgue decomposition relative to $P_0$ is the unique
decomposition
$P_1=P_{1,\mathrm{ac}}+P_{1,\mathrm{s}}$ with
$P_{1,\mathrm{ac}}\ll P_0$ and $P_{1,\mathrm{s}}\perp P_0$
([[thm-lebesgue-decomposition-exists-for-sigma-finite-signed-measures]],
[[thm-lebesgue-decomposition-is-unique-for-sigma-finite-signed-measures]]).
Both components are positive by
[[lem-positive-lebesgue-components-of-a-positive-measure]], and
$P_{1,\mathrm{ac}}$ is finite because their sum has mass one. Define the
**likelihood-ratio density** of $P_1$ against $P_0$ to be the
$P_0$-almost-everywhere class
$$
\frac{dP_{1,\mathrm{ac}}}{dP_0}
$$
of [[def-radon-nikodym-derivative]]. Under AC this class has a nonnegative
measurable representative by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].

This is a full density of $P_1$ with respect to $P_0$ only in the
absolutely continuous case $P_1\ll P_0$. If that condition fails, the
singular component remains separate. A displayed representative is not a
canonical pointwise function: its values are determined only
$P_0$-almost everywhere.

Assume AC and let $P_0,P_1$ be probability measures on one measurable space.
Let $r$ be a nonnegative measurable representative of the likelihood-ratio
class for $P_1$ versus $P_0$. If $P_1\ll P_0$, then
$$
E_{P_0}[g r]=E_{P_1}[g]
$$
for every nonnegative measurable $g$, and also for every real-valued
$P_1$-integrable measurable $g$. Here $E_{P_i}[h]$ means
$\int h\,dP_i$. Without $P_1\ll P_0$, this identity need not hold because the
singular component may be nonzero.

$f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. The **measure with density $f$ relative
to $\mu$** is the measure
$$f\,d\mu:\mathcal A\to[0,+\infty],\qquad (f\,d\mu)(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu,$$
whose measure property is supplied by
The indefinite integral of a nonnegative measurable function is a measure.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ and $(Y,\mathcal{B})$ be measurable spaces
(Measurable spaces and measurable sets). A function $f : X \to Y$ is **measurable** when

$$f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \qquad \text{for every } B \in \mathcal{B}.$$

Equivalently, the family

$$\mathcal{C}_f := \{\, B \subseteq Y : f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \,\}$$

is a sigma-algebra on $Y$ containing $\mathcal{B}$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

1. If $f,g:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ are measurable and $f+g$ is defined
   pointwise, then $f+g$ is measurable.
2. If $c\in\mathbb R$ and $f:X\to\mathbb R$ is measurable, then $cf$ is
   measurable.
3. If $f:X\to\mathbb R$ is measurable, then $f^+=\max\{f,0\}$,
   $f^-=\max\{-f,0\}$, and $|f|=f^++f^-$ are measurable.
4. If $E\in\mathcal A$ and $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, then
   $f\chi_E$ is measurable, where this function equals $f$ on $E$ and $0$
   off $E$ (in particular, $0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ here).
5. If $(f_n)$ is a sequence of measurable functions $X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$,
   then $\inf_n f_n$ is measurable; if moreover $f_n\uparrow f$ pointwise, then
   $f$ is measurable.

$\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal P(X)$ closed under binary intersections: if
$A,B\in\mathcal P$, then $A\cap B\in\mathcal P$.

The nonempty-family requirement is the convention used here. It does not require
$X\in\mathcal P$ and it does not add an empty-intersection axiom.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
Measurable rectangles in a product of measurable spaces.

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $(\mathsf X,\Sigma_X)$, $(\mathsf Y,\Sigma_Y)$, and $(\mathsf A,\Sigma_A)$ be nonempty measurable spaces. A **source/target pair of joint laws** consists of probability measures $P_S$ and $P_T$ on $(\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y,\Sigma_X\otimes\Sigma_Y)$. For $D\in\{S,T\}$, its input marginal is the probability measure $\mu_D$ on $(\mathsf X,\Sigma_X)$ defined by $\mu_D(A)=P_D(A\times\mathsf Y)$. If $h:\mathsf X\to\mathsf A$ is measurable and $\ell:\mathsf A\times\mathsf Y\to[0,+\infty]$ is product-measurable, then $(x,y)\mapsto(h(x),y)$ is measurable: the preimage of a measurable rectangle $U\times V$ is $h^{-1}(U)\times V$, and such rectangles generate the product sigma-algebra. Taking preimages once more shows that $(x,y)\mapsto\ell(h(x),y)$ is measurable. The domain risk is the extended nonnegative integral
$$R_D(h):=\int_{\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y}\ell(h(x),y)\,P_D(d(x,y)).$$

A **conditional label kernel** for $P_D$ is a specified probability kernel $K_D$ from $(\mathsf X,\Sigma_X)$ to $(\mathsf Y,\Sigma_Y)$ such that, for every nonnegative product-measurable $g:\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y\to[0,+\infty]$,
$$\int g(x,y)\,P_D(d(x,y))=\int_{\mathsf X}\left(\int_{\mathsf Y}g(x,y)\,K_D(x,dy)\right)\mu_D(dx).$$
The pair is under **covariate shift** when conditional label kernels $K_S,K_T$ are supplied, there is a measurable set $N$ with $\mu_T(N)=0$ such that $K_S(x,\cdot)=K_T(x,\cdot)$ as probability measures for every $x\notin N$, and $\mu_T\ll\mu_S$. No existence of conditional kernels is asserted by this definition.

Let $\mathcal E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be dominated by the fixed sigma-finite positive measure $\mu$. For each
$\theta$, the Radon–Nikodym theorem gives the almost-everywhere class
$dP_\theta/d\mu$; a sigma-finite exhaustion for $\mu$ is also finite for the
probability measure $P_\theta$. Under AC, select simultaneously a
finite-valued measurable nonnegative representative $p_\theta$ from each
class. The nonnegative version exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].

For fixed observed $x\in\mathcal X$, the function
$$L_x:\Theta\to[0,+\infty),\qquad L_x(\theta):=p_\theta(x),$$
is the **likelihood at $x$**. This is a function on the parameter labels, not
a probability distribution on $\Theta$. No sigma-algebra on $\Theta$ or
measurability of $L_x$ is implied. Each density is determined only
$\mu$-almost everywhere; there is no canonical pointwise version and, for
arbitrary uncountable $\Theta$, no common exceptional null set is asserted.

Assume AC. Let $P_S,P_T$ be source and target joint laws with input marginals $\mu_S,\mu_T$ and specified conditional label kernels $K_S,K_T$ as in the definition of source/target distributions. Suppose $\mu_T\ll\mu_S$ and there is a $\mu_T$-null set outside of which $K_S(x,\cdot)=K_T(x,\cdot)$. Let $w$ be any nonnegative measurable representative of $d\mu_T/d\mu_S$. Then for every product-measurable set $E\subseteq\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y$,
$$P_T(E)=\int_E w(x)\,P_S(d(x,y)).$$
Consequently $P_T\ll P_S$ and $w\circ\pi_X$ is a representative of the likelihood-ratio density of $P_T$ with respect to $P_S$.

In a supervised prediction problem, for every measurable predictor $f$, the function $(x,y)\mapsto\ell(f(x),y)$ is measurable, so its population risk is a defined extended nonnegative integral. For every sample size $m\ge1$, the empirical risk $S\mapsto\widehat R_S(f)$ is an extended nonnegative measurable function on the finite product sample space.

Assume AC and let $P_0,P_1$ be probability measures on one measurable space.
Let $r$ be a nonnegative measurable representative of the likelihood-ratio
class for $P_1$ versus $P_0$. If $P_1\ll P_0$, then
$$
E_{P_0}[g r]=E_{P_1}[g]
$$
for every nonnegative measurable $g$, and also for every real-valued
$P_1$-integrable measurable $g$. Here $E_{P_i}[h]$ means
$\int h\,dP_i$. Without $P_1\ll P_0$, this identity need not hold because the
singular component may be nonzero.

$$\operatorname{disc}_L(P,Q):=\sup_{h,h'\in\mathcal H}\left|L_P(h',h)-L_Q(h',h)\right|\in[0,+\infty].$$

A **source/target pair of joint laws** consists of probability measures $P_S$ and $P_T$ on $(\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y,\Sigma_X\otimes\Sigma_Y)$. For $D\in\{S,T\}$, its input marginal is the probability measure $\mu_D$ on $(\mathsf X,\Sigma_X)$ defined by $\mu_D(A)=P_D(A\times\mathsf Y)$. If $h:\mathsf X\to\mathsf A$ is measurable and $\ell:\mathsf A\times\mathsf Y\to[0,+\infty]$ is product-measurable, then $(x,y)\mapsto(h(x),y)$ is measurable: the preimage of a measurable rectangle $U\times V$ is $h^{-1}(U)\times V$, and such rectangles generate the product sigma-algebra. Taking preimages once more shows that $(x,y)\mapsto\ell(h(x),y)$ is measurable. The domain risk is the extended nonnegative integral
$$R_D(h):=\int_{\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y}\ell(h(x),y)\,P_D(d(x,y)).$$

A **conditional label kernel** for $P_D$ is a specified probability kernel $K_D$ from $(\mathsf X,\Sigma_X)$ to $(\mathsf Y,\Sigma_Y)$ such that, for every nonnegative product-measurable $g:\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y\to[0,+\infty]$,
$$\int g(x,y)\,P_D(d(x,y))=\int_{\mathsf X}\left(\int_{\mathsf Y}g(x,y)\,K_D(x,dy)\right)\mu_D(dx).$$
The pair is under **covariate shift** when conditional label kernels $K_S,K_T$ are supplied, there is a measurable set $N$ with $\mu_T(N)=0$ such that $K_S(x,\cdot)=K_T(x,\cdot)$ as probability measures for every $x\notin N$, and $\mu_T\ll\mu_S$. No existence of conditional kernels is asserted by this definition.

Let $(\mathsf X,\Sigma_X)$ be a measurable space, equip $\{0,1\}$ with its discrete sigma-algebra, let $\mu_S$ and $\mu_T$ be probability measures on $\mathsf X$, and let $\mathcal H$ be a nonempty class of measurable classifiers $h:\mathsf X\to\{0,1\}$. $$A_{h,h'}:=\bigl(h^{-1}(\{0\})\cap h'^{-1}(\{1\})\bigr)\cup\bigl(h^{-1}(\{1\})\cap h'^{-1}(\{0\})\bigr).$$
